These gains persist as the per-qubit port budget grows, with RELIQ still reducing the depth by 71.7% and 51.2% at $16$ ports, suggesting these heuristics remain relevant even as hardware exposes more access points.

papers.title: Non-Maximally Entangled States for Quantum Key Distribution in Underwater Channels: BBM92 Protocol via Kraus Operators
papers.abstract: Underwater optical channels pose significant challenges to the security and reliability of quantum communication systems due to absorption and scattering. In this paper, we investigate the BBM92 entanglement-based quantum key distribution (EBQKD) protocol under realistic conditions over a non-turbulent underwater channel. Photon pairs are prepared in non-maximally entangled states, and the underwater propagation medium is modeled as a quantum channel composed of a polarization-independent photon-loss channel and a depolarizing channel, described within the Kraus operator formalism. The protocol performance is evaluated in terms of quantum correlations, quantum bit error rate (QBER) and secret key rate (SKR), analyzed as functions of the entanglement degree and channel degradation parameters. We derived analytical expressions for the quantum correlations, the QBER and the SKR over the proposed channel model, and validated them through Monte Carlo simulations. The proposed framework is then applied to various realistic underwater scenarios, considering different water types, namely clear ocean, coastal, and turbid water, as well as varying atmospheric conditions.

papers.title: Insights Generator: Systematic Corpus-Level Trace Diagnostics for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Diagnosing failures in LLM agents remains largely manual. Practitioners inspect a small subset of execution traces, form ad-hoc hypotheses, and iterate. This process misses patterns that only emerge across trace populations and does not scale to production corpora where individual traces span tens of thousands of tokens. We formalize the problem of corpus-level trace diagnostics. Given a corpus of execution traces, the goal is to produce grounded natural-language insights that characterize systematic behavioral patterns across trace groups, each linked to supporting evidence. We present the Insights Generator (IG), a multi-agent system that answers diagnostic questions by proposing and testing hypotheses across the trace corpus to produce an evidence-backed insights report. We evaluate IG across qualitative and objective dimensions, spanning rubric-based report assessment and downstream performance improvements achieved by implementing IG insights. Human experts using IG reports improve scaffold performance by 30.4 pp over the unmodified baseline scaffold, and coding agents leveraging IG-derived insights show consistent and stable gains. Across benchmarks, IG's scout-investigator architecture produces findings comparable in detection coverage to competing approaches, while domain experts rated IG reports as leading depth and evidence quality.

papers.title: Eyes on VLM: Benchmarking Gaze Following and Social Gaze Prediction in Vision Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have rapidly evolved into general-purpose multimodal reasoners with strong zero-shot generalization. In this context, VLMs could greatly benefit the analysis of human gaze and attention, a central task in human behavior understanding that requires reasoning about the physical scene as well as the activity, interactions, and social context. However, the extent to which VLMs can reliably understand human gaze and related attentional behaviors remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present EyeVLM, a systematic evaluation framework for gaze understanding in VLMs across two complementary dimensions: tasks and models. To assess gaze understanding capabilities, we focus on two core tasks. The first, gaze following, i.e., predicting the 2D location where a person is looking, has a geometric and visual processing focus, requiring a precise understanding of the human face, attention direction, 3D scene structure, and spatial grounding of attended targets. The second, social gaze prediction, requires social and relational reasoning over multi-person interactions (e.g., mutual gaze and shared attention), and may benefit more from the LLM semantic reasoning capabilities within VLMs. Regarding models, EyeVLM evaluates these tasks in two ways: a zero-shot setting with a diverse set of state-of-the-art open- and closed-source VLMs, exploring different prompting strategies; and a fine-tuning approach based on task-specific QA pairs, studying the impact of model scale and data scale. As benchmarks, we rely on existing gaze understanding datasets and perform a systematic comparison with state-of-the-art purely visual models. Overall, our results show that current VLMs lack precise gaze understanding capabilities. While standard training helps reduce the gap with visual models, significant improvements are still needed. Code available at this https URL .

papers.title: Authors' Response to AI-Based Reviews: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
papers.abstract: Background: Large language models are increasingly used to assist scholarly peer review, but there is limited evidence about how authors judge their feedback and use it to revise their papers. Methods: We studied authors' experiences of receiving an auxiliary AI review alongside human reviews in three computer-science cohorts: LifeCLEF 2025, LifeCLEF 2026, and CVWW 2026. Post-review questionnaires yielded 92 responses concerning 71 papers. We summarized closed-ended answers using descriptive statistics and examined free-text responses through thematic analysis. Results: Most responses rated the AI review useful (82/92 (89%), and 82/92 (89%) reported using at least some of its suggestions in revision. Authors reported that AI identified issues missed by human reviewers ((76/92 (83%). However, 44/92 (48%) trusted AI feedback less than human feedback, and 58/92 (63%) reported incorrect or misleading comments. Authors valued suggestions that improved clarity and reproducibility, but also described overlooked evidence, inappropriate demands, and difficulty finding useful comments within lengthy reviews. They emphasized the need to check AI feedback and retain control over how their manuscripts were processed. Future review by both humans and AI was supported by 85/92 (92%); 83/92 (90%) preferred advance notice and 73/92 (79%) supported explicit consent. Conclusions: Authors often found AI reviews useful for revision without trusting them as much as human reviews. These exploratory findings favor a supplementary role for AI, with human oversight, clear disclosure, and author consent. They do not establish that AI can replace human reviewers or improve manuscript quality.

papers.title: MyoChallenge 2025: A New Benchmark for Human Athletic Intelligence
papers.abstract: Athletic performance represents the pinnacle of human motor intelligence, demanding rapid choices, precise control, agility, and coordinated physical execution. Replicating this seamless combination of capabilities remains elusive in current artificial intelligence and robotic systems. Concurrently, understanding the biological mastery of these movements is hindered because complex muscle coordination is rarely measured in vivo due to the limitations of physical equipment. To bridge this fundamental gap in understanding, MyoChallenge at NeurIPS 2025 established a pioneering benchmark for motor control intelligence in sports, leveraging high-fidelity musculoskeletal models within physics simulation combined with machine learning-driven algorithms. The competition introduces two distinct tracks emphasizing either upper or lower limbs control: a table tennis rally task utilizing a biomechanic upper limb composed of an arm with a hand and a trunk; and a soccer penalty kick using a biomechanic model of legs and a trunk. Marking the fourth iteration of the MyoChallenge series, this event attracted almost 70 teams and over 560 submissions globally, uniting a diverse community ranging from physicians and neuroscientists to machine learning experts. The competition facilitated the development of several state-of-the-art control algorithms for a musculoskeletal system capable of sports agility, leveraging techniques such as physics-based motion planners, on-policy behaviour cloning, hierarchical planning, and muscle synergies. By integrating standardized tasks and physiologically realistic models into the open-source framework of MyoSuite, MyoChallenge'25 serves as a reproducible and reusable testbed to accelerate interdisciplinary research across machine learning, biomechanics, sports science, and neuroscience. Project page: this https URL .

papers.title: Spectral Vision Transformer for Efficient Tokenization with Limited Data
papers.abstract: Vision transformers tokenize an image into patches, which couples the token count to resolution and requires the embedding to be learned from data. We propose a spectral vision transformer architecture for efficient tokenization in the limited-data regime, with an emphasis on medical imaging. Rather than using spatial patches, we tokenize into coefficients of a fixed basis. This approach defines each token as one spectral mode, and the sequence length is chosen rather than implied by resolution, reducing the cost of attention. Our proposed spectral ViT shows superior or comparable performance where data is scarce in public medical imaging benchmarks, natural images, object shapes, simulations, and protected clinical data. We release our code at: this https URL .

papers.title: Behavioral Integrity Verification for AI Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Agent skills extend LLM agents with privileged third-party capabilities such as filesystem access, credentials, network calls, and shell execution. Existing safety work catches malicious prompts and risky runtime actions, but the skill artifact itself goes unverified. We formalize this as the behavioral integrity verification (BIV) problem: a typed set comparison between declared and actual capabilities over a shared taxonomy that bridges code, instructions, and metadata. The BIV framework instantiates this comparison by pairing deterministic code analysis with LLM-assisted capability extraction. The resulting structured evidence supports three downstream analyses: deviation taxonomy, root-cause classification, and malicious-skill detection. On 49,943 skills from the OpenClaw registry, the deviation taxonomy reveals a pervasive description-implementation gap: 80.0% of skills have at least one deviation in the taxonomy, with four compound-threat categories surfaced. Root-cause classification finds that deviations are mostly oversight, not malice: 81.1% trace to developer oversight and 18.9% to adversarial intent, with 5.0% of skills carrying predicted multi-stage attack chains. On a 906-skill malicious-skill detection benchmark, BIV reaches an F1 of 0.949, outperforming state-of-the-art rule-based and single-pass LLM baselines. These results demonstrate behavioral integrity auditing for agent skills at scale.

papers.title: Algorithms for Computing Set Tolerances: Theory, Computational Analysis and Applications
papers.abstract: The regular set tolerance is an important term in sensitivity analysis. For combinatorial sum problems, e.g., the Traveling Salesman Problem, Shortest Path Problem and Minimum Spanning Tree Problem, it determines how much the sum of the costs of the elements of a set can be increased while ensuring that all current optimal solutions remain optimal. The regular set lower tolerance determines how much the sum of the costs of the elements of a set can be decreased while ensuring that the objective value of the optimal solution is not changed. We investigate general methods for computing regular (upper and lower) set tolerances in combinatorial sum problems. For the upper tolerance, we present a linear programming approach, and for the lower tolerances, three linear programming approaches, where the last two are novel and lead to recursive procedures for computation of the lower tolerances of all subsets of the given ground set. We give new upper bounds for set lower tolerances. For both upper and lower tolerances, we give an exact formula for sets of cardinality 2 and 3. Furthermore, we computationally compare and analyze our introduced tolerance LPs. Finally, we consider the computation of tolerances for the Minimum Spanning Tree Problem, give a formula for single tolerances, a lower bound for regular set upper tolerances and an exact formula for regular set lower tolerances.

papers.title: STEPSIC: Initial condition generator for stereographic cosmological simulations
papers.abstract: We present STEPSIC, an open-source initial condition generator for cosmological N-body simulations in the periodic cuboid, spherical, and cylindrical geometries supported by StePS. It succeeds the earlier StePS initial condition code and extends it to periodic cuboids with arbitrary aspect ratios and cylindrical topologies. Gaussian density fields are generated on a periodic Fourier grid. First- and second-order Lagrangian perturbation theory (LPT) displacements and velocities are interpolated to lattices or relaxed glasses with radially varying particle masses. For spherical and cylindrical domains, an enclosing periodic box supplies the fields, and a multiresolution scheme matches resolved wavelengths to local particle mass. With identical white noise, the periodic calculation agrees with monofonIC to within $0.05\%$ in power spectrum and $0.15\%$ in median particle displacement. On relaxed spherical and cylindrical glasses, comparison with independent sums over retained Fourier modes gives errors consistent with linear interpolation. For an enclosing box of one domain diameter, the root-mean-square relative displacement of two points in the high-resolution region differs from the infinite-Universe value by at most $0.0014\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ out of $0.5\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ at $z=31$, while domain-scale mean-density variance is suppressed. In one cylindrical realization evolved to $z=0$, doubling the enclosing box shifts the high-resolution region by $0.39\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$; after removing this bulk displacement, power spectra differ by at most $1.05\%$. In a cylindrical StePS simulation evolved to $z=0$, first-order initial conditions leave up to $3.6\%$ less nonlinear power than second-order ones, consistent with LPT transients.

papers.title: Spherical Boltzmann machines: a solvable theory of learning and generation in energy-based models
papers.abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) are flexible generative architectures inspired by statistical physics, but their learning and generative properties remain poorly understood. Here, we analyze a solvable EBM in the high-dimensional limit: the spherical Boltzmann machine (SBM). Combining tools from random matrix theory and dynamical mean-field theory, we: derive and solve closed equations describing the training dynamics of the SBM in the high-dimensional limit; compute the asymptotic Bayesian evidence, which acts as a partition function in parameter space and encodes global properties of the trained model; and uncover cascades of phase transitions that occur both during training and as a function of hyperparameters, related to successive alignment and condensation of the top modes of the coupling matrix to the data. We connect these transitions to sampling-time generative phenomena in a teacher-student scenario, including: sampling temperature tuning, double descent as a function of regularization strength, tempered posterior effects, and out-of-equilibrium effects during training that induce biases in the trained model. We provide numerical evidence showing that all these phenomena appear in standard generative architectures, beyond the SBM.

papers.title: Post-Reasoning: Improving the Performance of Non-Thinking Models at Negligible Cost
papers.abstract: As the widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) accelerates, token consumption from intermediate reasoning traces increasingly contributes to inference latency and operational cost. Recent studies suggest that many real-world tasks require little to no explicit reasoning, with additional reasoning sometimes even degrading performance. In this work, we propose Post-Reasoning, a simple yet effective approach that improves instruction-tuned models by conditioning them to justify their answers after generating the final response. By design, it enables the final answer to be obtained with no reasoning tokens before the answer and with negligible latency and token cost, while still improving performance through simple instruction augmentation. We evaluate Post-Reasoning across 117 model benchmark settings spanning 13 open and proprietary models, 7 model families, and 9 diverse reasoning and knowledge-intensive benchmarks, including AMC, HMMT, GSM8K, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and BIG-Bench Hard. Post-Reasoning improves performance in 84.62% of evaluated settings, achieving a mean relative improvement of 15.57%. Furthermore, we propose supervised post-reason tuning, which further improves performance in 91.11% of evaluated settings, and exceeds the prompt-based post-reasoning baseline by an average of 7.17%, demonstrating that post-reasoning can be effectively internalized through training. Ultimately, Post-Reasoning establishes a new performance ceiling for direct-answer capabilities.

papers.title: A minimal probe of task modeling in language models
papers.abstract: Language models read long contexts and score well on knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, but neither shows whether a model can do work whose next step depends on everything that came before, as a long-running agent must. We call this ability task modeling and propose counting identical items as its simplest test: every item adds to the total and no item records it. We define counting capacity (CC) as the sequence length up to which a model returns the exact count more often than not, and measure it for 205 models. Every resolved measurement loses count abruptly, at a median of 50 items and at most 627; across release years the median rose 1.6-fold while context windows grew about 80-fold. Changing the counted symbol or the delimiter moves a model's CC severalfold, yet the model accounts for about three quarters of the variance across 16 models and 11 encodings. Reasoning leaves the median CC unchanged across 77 matched pairs. In six open-weight models the count stays readable in early layers past the boundary but does not reach the output, and an activation edit that carries the count forward also carries the state of an object-tracking task. CC tracks the METR task horizon after controlling for general capability, and rises with capacity on grid-execution tasks and, with reasoning off, on object tracking. We do not show that counting is necessary or sufficient for long-horizon work; that remains a hypothesis, which this cheap measurement can test.

papers.title: Supercriticality of the SIRS on random networks
papers.abstract: We analyze the supercritical regime of the SIRS process (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Susceptible) on random graphs and Galton-Watson trees. Our results provide a three-part characterization of this process: first, we prove that even on finite sparse graphs, the epidemic can survive for an exponentially long time. On heavy-tailed networks with power-law-like exponents, we show that this holds for the entire range of parameters. Notably, while contemporary works establish a stretched exponential survival time for power-law networks, our approach provides the optimal bound of order $e^{\Theta(n)}$ via a different approach. Finally, for infinite trees, we establish sufficient conditions for strong survival, proving that the root is re-infected infinitely often even for light-tailed degree distributions like the Poisson distribution.

papers.title: Component-Adaptive and Lesion-Level Supervision for Improved Small Structure Segmentation in Brain MRI
papers.abstract: Small lesions in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are easily missed: a segmentation model can reach a high Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) while leaving many of them undetected. We ask whether this omission comes from the network or from the training objective. In multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation, nnU-Net trained with its default Dice and cross-entropy loss produces almost no response to most of the small lesions it misses, so no decision threshold recovers them, and four other architectures trained with the same loss detect no more of them. We therefore change only the objective. CATMIL adds two lesion-level terms to the nnU-Net loss: a Component-Adaptive Tversky (CAT) term, which gives each lesion a weight nearly independent of its size, and a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) term, which treats each lesion as a bag of voxels and penalizes any lesion in which no voxel is detected. On MSLesSeg, CATMIL raises small-lesion recall from 0.796 to 0.873 (difference 95\% CI +0.030 to +0.157) and misses 48\% fewer lesions, at comparable DSC. The gain holds on the cross-validation predictions of 47 further patients, for lesions of at least 3~mm, and on a second dataset trained with the same loss weights. CATMIL also detects more small lesions than CC-DiceCE, an instance-level loss that balances lesions within an overlap term (0.873 vs.\ 0.831), indicating that lesions must be supervised not only in proportion but also for their detection. The cost is additional small false-positive components; a component-size filter removes most of them, and at the lesion-wise precision of the default loss CATMIL still detects more small lesions. Code: this https URL .

papers.title: A Partially Parabolic Damage-Driven Inflammation Model: Threshold Dynamics and Linear Spreading
papers.abstract: We study a partially parabolic reaction--diffusion--chemotaxis model of damage--inflammation feedback motivated by Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The model couples functional and damaged tissue with effective macrophage activity and a damage-induced inflammatory signal. The invariant tissue simplex bounds the damage source and, together with parabolic estimates, yields global well-posedness and dissipativity in every spatial dimension covered by the regularity assumptions, for arbitrary chemotactic sensitivity. A dimensionless feedback threshold separates resolution to a damage-free dystrophin-deficient state from the existence of a positive damage equilibrium in the spatially homogeneous system. On bounded connected domains, we prove resolution at and below the threshold and, above it, uniform componentwise persistence with spatially uniform lower bounds for initial data with at least one nonzero active component. We derive a candidate linear spreading speed for localized damage and establish a nonlinear upper spreading bound in the absence of chemotaxis. Numerical front speeds agree closely with the linear prediction in the simulations.

papers.title: The Bollobás--Nikiforov inequality for complete multipartite graphs, with remarks on the $K_4$-free case
papers.abstract: Bollobás and Nikiforov conjectured that every graph $G \neq K_n$ with $m$ edges and clique number $\omega$ satisfies $\lambda_1^2(G) + \lambda_2^2(G) \leq 2(1 - 1/\omega)m$, where $\lambda_1(G) \geq \lambda_2(G)$ are the two largest adjacency eigenvalues. We give a short self-contained proof of the inequality for complete multipartite graphs, based on a quadratic-form identity which shows that $\lambda_2 \leq 0$, and we determine the equality cases in this class. We show that equality in the conjecture is attained by a wider family than the Turán graphs, namely by disjoint unions of two complete bipartite graphs, or of two balanced complete $r$-partite graphs of possibly different orders. For $K_4$-free graphs we record the cases that follow from known results, with corrected attributions, and we give examples showing that three natural lines of attack fail: a Hoffman-type eigenvalue bound for graphs with large independence number, a spectral stability statement for connected graphs, and Zykov symmetrization in an arbitrary direction.

papers.title: p-Adic Dirac Equations and the Jackiw-Rebbi Model
papers.abstract: We present a p-adic version of the Jackiw-Rebbi model, in which the real line is replaced by the p-adic numbers and the Dirac Hamiltonian by a non-local operator built from the twisted Vladimirov operator. We show that p-adic quantum mechanics, although non-local, yields a physical picture that agrees with the Archimedean one, realized through mechanisms with no Archimedean counterpart. The agreement is specific: for a constant mass the p-adic model is gapped, with the same gap; it has a chiral symmetry, so its spectrum is symmetric about zero energy; a change of sign of the mass binds states at an interface; and at low energies its spectrum cannot be distinguished from the Archimedean continuous spectrum. The mechanisms are not: the p-adic free Hamiltonian is diagonalized by compactly supported wavelets, so every stationary state is strictly localized; momentum takes values on a geometric ladder of powers of the prime; and a zero-energy interface state exists only for masses commensurate with that ladder. The standard Dirac equation does not admit space-localized solutions because it contradicts Einstein's causality. The model is realizable at every finite resolution, as a continuous-time quantum walk, and the topological protection of the Archimedean zero mode is lost.

papers.title: Cohen-Macaulay squarefree powers of edge ideals of very well-covered graphs
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a graph with edge ideal $I(G)$. For $q\ge 1$, the $q$th squarefree power $I(G)^{[q]}$ is the Stanley-Reisner ideal of the $q$-matching-free complex $\mathsf{MF}^q(G)$, whose faces are the vertex sets containing no $q$ pairwise disjoint edges. We determine exactly which squarefree powers of the edge ideal of a very well-covered graph are Cohen-Macaulay: if $G$ has $2n$ vertices, then $R/I(G)^{[q]}$ is Cohen-Macaulay if and only if $q=n$, or $q=1$ and $G$ is Cohen-Macaulay, or $G=W(H)$ is a whisker graph and $q \le \left\lfloor \frac{\operatorname{girth}(H)}{2} \right\rfloor$. The answer is independent of the field. The proof rests on a rigidity theorem: among very well-covered graphs, only whisker graphs have a sequentially Cohen-Macaulay squarefree power strictly between the first and the last. For whisker graphs we show that $\mathsf{MF}^q(W(H))$ is vertex decomposable for $q \le \left\lceil \frac{\operatorname{girth}(H)}{2} \right\rceil$, and we express the depth and the regularity of every squarefree power through the homology of explicit auxiliary complexes. As a consequence we prove a conjecture of Das, Roy and Saha on the depth of squarefree powers of whisker cycles. Finally, for every graph with a perfect matching, we compute the top homology of $\mathsf{MF}^q(G)$ and determine when the regularity of $R/I(G)^{[q]}$ attains its maximal possible value.

papers.title: Learning Object-Centric Spatial Reasoning for Sequential Manipulation in Cluttered Environments
papers.abstract: Sequential manipulation in clutter requires selecting which objects to remove and determining how to manipulate them. Learning both decisions jointly can complicate training and make failures difficult to diagnose. We present Unveiler, a modular framework that separates scene reasoning and object selection from action execution through a discrete object-index interface. Its Spatial Relationship Encoder (SRE) selects the best object to grasp, while a separate Action Decoder generates orientation-discretized push-grasp actions. The SRE is trained in two stages: imitation learning from heuristic demonstrations, followed by search-based policy improvement using simulated object removals. This training procedure requires no real-robot training data and allows the SRE to be paired with a different execution policy. We evaluate Unveiler in PyBullet simulation and on a physical Dofbot-Pro. In real-robot experiments, it retrieves two occluded targets in the prescribed order in 90\% of scenes, compared with 20-30\% for the heuristic, GPT-4o, and the imitation-only variant. In PyBullet, Unveiler achieves the highest task-completion rate across all six clutter-density and occlusion conditions, reaching 90.0\% under full occlusion with 6-9 objects, compared with 67.5\% for the heuristic and 60.0\% for ThinkGrasp. These results demonstrate the potential of modular, object-centric spatial reasoning for sequential manipulation in clutter.

papers.title: An Autonomous Sea Turtle Robot that Follows Marine Animals
papers.abstract: Autonomous robots can transform how we observe marine ecosystems, enabling vision-based focal follows (animal tracking) at scale, but close-range operation in reefs and other cluttered habitats remains difficult. Vehicles must maneuver safely near animals and fragile structures while coping with currents, variable lighting and limited sensing. Previous approaches simplify these problems by leveraging soft materials and bioinspired swimming designs, but such platforms remain limited in terms of deployable autonomy. Here we present an approach to vision-based autonomy that advances the state of the art in biomimetic marine robots and we demonstrate our approach on a sea turtle-inspired underwater robot. The robot combines robust depth-heading stabilization with obstacle avoidance and target-centric control, enabling it to track and interact with moving objects in complex terrain. We validate the approach in controlled pool experiments and in an artificial coral reef at the New England Aquarium, demonstrating stable operation and reliable tracking of fast-moving marine animals. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first integrated biomimetic robotic system, combining novel hardware, control, and field experiments, deployed to autonomously follow real marine animals. With all perception and control running onboard, the robot can hold a commanded depth, navigate around obstacles (91% success rate in the aquarium exhibit with complex lighting and visual features including glass panels) and successfully identify and follow sea turtles fully autonomously. An additional operator-initialized tracking mode extends beyond just sea turtles, including fast-moving rays, barracuda, and human divers. Together, these results establish a practical route toward bioinspired underwater robots capable of autonomous exploration and close-range animal monitoring in sensitive ecosystems.

papers.title: Exponential Lower Bounds for 2-query Relaxed Locally Decodable Codes
authors: Minshen Zhu ((1) University of Illinois at Chicago
papers.abstract: Locally Decodable Codes (LDCs) are error-correcting codes $C\colon\Sigma^n\rightarrow \Sigma^m,$ encoding \emph{messages} in $\Sigma^n$ to \emph{codewords} in $\Sigma^m$, with super-fast decoding algorithms. They are important mathematical objects in many areas of theoretical computer science, yet the best constructions so far have codeword length $m$ that is super-polynomial in $n$, for codes with constant query complexity and constant alphabet size, while tolerating a constant-fraction of errors. In a very surprising result, Ben-Sasson, Goldreich, Harsha, Sudan, and Vadhan (SICOMP 2006) show how to construct a relaxed version of LDCs (RLDCs) with constant query complexity and slightly super-linear codeword length over the binary alphabet, and used them to obtain significantly-improved constructions of Probabilistically Checkable Proofs. In this work, we prove an exponential lower bound on the length of Hamming RLDCs making $2$ queries (even adaptively) over the binary alphabet. This answers a question explicitly raised by Gur and Lachish (SICOMP 2021) and is the first exponential lower bound for RLDCs. Combined with the results of Ben-Sasson et al., our result exhibits a "phase-transition"-type behavior on the codeword length for some constant-query complexity. We achieve these lower bounds via a transformation of RLDCs to LDCs, using a careful analysis of restrictions of message bits that fix codeword bits.

papers.title: Countability Properties of Weakly Compact Sets in Asymmetric Locally Convex Spaces
papers.abstract: A dual pair formulation for asymmetric locally convex spaces is introduced that strictly generalises the ordinary vector space setting. The concept of a polar topology carries over to the asymmetric case and some familiar results are reproduced or generalised such as the bipolar theorem and a Mackey-Arens type theorem. The implications of weak compactness and countability properties are studied and appear intimately connected to separation properties. An asymmetric analogue $C_a(K)$ of the well-known space $C_p(K)$ is introduced and the properties of (relatively) countably respectively sequentially) compact subspaces are investigated. In particular, it is shown that $C_a([0,1])$ is not angelic. However, for Hausdorff subspaces, the different compactness conditions are equivalent and imply the Fréchet-Urysohn property. Moreover, an analogue of the Eberlein-Šmulian theorem holds in asymmetrically normed spaces.

papers.title: Wedge Sampling: Efficient Tensor Completion with Nearly-Linear Sample Complexity
papers.abstract: We introduce wedge sampling, a non-adaptive sampling scheme for recovering an order-$k$ low-rank tensor of side length $n$ from structured observations of its entries. The scheme samples pairs of entries in the same column of a tensor unfolding, forming length-two paths (wedges) in the associated bipartite sampling graph. The products of the paired entries supply the row correlations needed for spectral initialization in regimes where uniform sampling yields too few wedges. For fixed rank, incoherence, tensor order, and condition number, wedge sampling enables polynomial-time recovery with nearly linear sample complexity in $n$. The spectral initializer can be combined with existing refinement procedures using only an additional $\tilde O(n)$ uniformly sampled entries. Spectral refinement achieves weak recovery to any fixed relative Frobenius error. For symmetric third-order tensors with incoherent canonical polyadic factors, gradient descent achieves exact recovery in the noiseless setting, with error decreasing geometrically. The improvement over the $\tilde O(n^{k/2})$ sample complexity typical of efficient methods under uniform entry sampling shows how the conjectured computational barrier depends on the observation model. A key ingredient for the gradient descent analysis is a concentration bound for sparse random tensors in an incoherent spectral norm. We also give error bounds for both procedures under additive Gaussian noise and explicit signal-to-noise conditions. Beyond tensor completion, the same sampling scheme improves the sample complexity of one-sided matrix completion, where the goal is to recover the left singular subspace of a matrix with many more columns than rows.

papers.title: Transitive Sets of Mutually Orthogonal Latin Squares
papers.abstract: Write $n=\prod_{i=1}^u p_i^{a_i}$ for the prime factorization of $n$. We prove that a net of order $n$ admitting a point-transitive group of automorphisms preserving each parallel class has at most $\min_i(p_i^{a_i}+1)$ parallel classes. This extends Jungnickel's sharp bound for translation nets. Equivalently, the maximum number of jointly cell-transitive mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order $n$ is $\min_i(p_i^{a_i}-1)$. An explicit Latin square of order nine answers affirmatively Krotov and Potapov's question about the existence of an isotopically transitive, non-topolinear Latin square.

papers.title: On the Damped Euler-Monge-Ampere equations with Radial Symmetry: Critical Thresholds and Large-Time Behavior
papers.abstract: We investigate the global well-posedness and large-time dynamics of the pressureless Euler-Monge-Ampere (EMA) system with velocity damping in multidimensions, subject to radially symmetric initial data. We first establish the phenomenon of critical thresholds, where subcritical initial data maintain global regularity, and supercritical initial data lead to finite time singularity formation. We provide two methods for constructing these thresholds: a refined spectral dynamics approach based on Liu and Tadmor (2002 Commun. Math. Phy. 228 435-66) and a comparison principle based on Lyapunov functions introduced in Bhatnagar and Liu (2020 Math. Models Methods Appl. Sci. 30 891-916). A key finding of this work is that the inclusion of linear damping effectively removes the initial density lower bound previously required in the undamped case (Tadmor and Tan 2022 SIAM J. Math. Anal. 54 4277-96) in certain regimes, allowing for global regularity even in the presence of vacuum or arbitrarily low density. Furthermore, for subcritical initial data, we prove an exponential decay rate to the equilibrium state. Our results unify and extend existing theories for 1D Euler-Poisson system and undamped multidimensional EMA system with radial symmetry.

papers.title: Virasoro Symmetry in Neural Network Field Theories
papers.abstract: We construct the Virasoro algebra from a neural free-field architecture. A logarithmic momentum law and a smooth spectral window give the weight-one current kernel, whose radial-ordering discontinuity fixes the oscillator pairing. The limiting neural current correlations agree with the Fock vacuum correlations. Their Sugawara stress tensor gives the Virasoro algebra with central charge one, and charged vertex insertions identify its highest-weight sectors. Bounds on regulator and feature errors control finite-mode approximations to this representation. At finite width, an explicit adjoint-compatible projection defines an auxiliary Fock readout when its Hermitian mixed block is positive. Cauchy features extend the construction to fermionic and supersymmetric sectors, including a Clifford zero mode in the Ramond representation, while first-order stress tensors give fermionic and bosonic ghost systems. Shared reflected features impose scalar boundary conditions in every realization and yield conformal and superconformal gluing in the limiting fields. Numerical comparisons support the current pairing and field correlations; their detailed analysis is collected in the appendices.

papers.title: Quantum Nondecimated Wavelet Transform: Theory, Circuits, and Applications
papers.abstract: The quantum nondecimated wavelet transform uses a shift register to apply circular shifts to an amplitude encoded signal before a single orthogonal wavelet transform. We show that tracing out the shift register gives level probabilities equal to the normalized nondecimated wavelet energies, invariant under circular shifts. Its diagonal gives moving averages of squared coefficients. We derive a multinomial model for the level counts and show how to read the autocovariance at lag one for all but the coarsest detail level. For these global statistics, direct Fourier basis measurement of the input is at least as precise and uses a simpler circuit. For denoising, we insert a block encoded shrinkage operator between the transform and its inverse. Postselection on the shift register implements the cycle spinning average exactly as a linear combination of unitaries. Weights shared within each level give a translation equivariant filter with zero phase. Local weights also preserve translation equivariance when indexed by the nondecimated translate. The circuit provides access to individual decimated branches and combines them coherently. We illustrate the method with James Stein shrinkage, local empirical Wiener filtering, and a scaling analysis of turbulent wind velocity. Gate simulations verify the construction, and we report state preparation, weight estimation, and output costs separately.

papers.title: Spectrally Robust Photon-Pair Generation in Topological Waveguide Arrays
papers.abstract: Harnessing topological effects offers a route to protect quantum states of light from imperfections, potentially enabling more robust platforms for quantum information processing. This capability is particularly relevant for active photonic circuits that generate quantum light directly on-chip. However, the impact of topology on the spectral properties of parametric processes, crucial for scalable quantum photonic circuits, remains largely unexplored. Here, we address this question by investigating photon-pair generation via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in nonlinear waveguide arrays, combining experiment and theory. A systematic comparison of uniform, trivial, and topological Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) arrays reveals that only the topological configuration preserves a stable SPDC resonance spectrum under coupling disorder, with fluctuations in the resonance wavelength reduced by more than an order of magnitude. An analytical model captures the origin of this robustness in the band-structure properties of the interacting modes. Numerical analysis further shows that each SSH array can operate as a robust photon-pair source, enabling stable interference between multiple such sources and the generation of high-dimensional entangled states with high fidelity. These results establish nonlinear waveguide arrays as a promising platform for harnessing the interplay of topology and nonlinearity in quantum photonic circuits.

papers.title: Does AI Assistance Preserve or Collapse Disagreement? A Study of Pre-Annotations in Ambiguous Video Labeling
papers.abstract: AI-generated Pre-Annotations can accelerate video labeling, but they may also anchor annotators to model priors and suppress disagreement that is valuable for pluralistic dataset construction. We study this tradeoff in ambiguous temporal video annotation, where annotators choose event boundaries and assign context-dependent labels such as "normal" or "abnormal." We introduce a controlled audit protocol that separates annotation cost, consensus alignment, inter-annotator consistency, temporal-boundary variation, semantic-label variation, latent-space standardization, and edit behavior. In a counterbalanced pilot study with 18 annotators and 180 annotation sessions, a fixed CLIP-based Pre-Annotation engine reduced mean annotation time by 23.11%; 72% of annotators were faster with assistance, with a median per-annotator gain of 35%. Assistance increased inter-annotator consistency and CLIP-space standardization, while semantic-label entropy changed only slightly in aggregate. A six-annotator human consensus diagnostic showed comparable alignment across conditions (AMI $\approx 0.64$ in both conditions), but this diagnostic is self-including and should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as independent evidence that model influence is absent. Overall, the results suggest that Pre-Annotations acted mainly as editable temporal scaffolds in this pilot setting, while leaving open the possibility of subtler semantic anchoring effects. We contribute an audit framework and anonymized interaction traces for studying when AI-assisted annotation preserves, reshapes, or collapses human disagreement.

papers.title: Benchmarking Robust Aggregation in Decentralized Gradient Marketplaces
papers.abstract: Institutions that cannot centralize or sell raw data increasingly exchange model updates instead: cross-silo federated learning is already in production among hospital networks and pharmaceutical consortia. A growing line of research targets the next step: marketplaces in which gradient updates are exchanged as paid, query-specific data products, though none is yet deployed at scale. We formalize this emerging paradigm as a Gradient Data Marketplace (GDM), in which data consumers issue learning tasks and distributed participants contribute query-specific gradient updates. Federated learning asks whether the model survives an attack; a marketplace must also ask who got paid. Existing protocols ensure model-level robustness but fail to capture whether high-quality data is correctly identified and rewarded. In a GDM, selection determines payment, incentivizing participants to optimize for inclusion rather than utility. We introduce a modular benchmarking framework that separates mechanism integrity (whether selection and payment reward true utility) from model integrity, and evaluate a standard baseline alongside 11 widely used aggregation mechanisms on five real-world vision, text, and tabular datasets. Our results reveal consistent adverse selection: honest high-variance contributions are rejected as outliers while strategically homogeneous malicious contributions are accepted and rewarded, even when model performance remains stable. These failures are not artifacts of our accounting: they persist under continuous, weight-proportional payment, compound across repeated market rounds as underpaid honest sellers exit, and worsen when honest sellers add differential-privacy noise, which the filters misread as contamination. Our benchmark provides a foundation for designing incentive-aware, auditable data selection mechanisms in emerging data marketplaces.

papers.title: Projected evolution of quantum gates for circuit simulation with matrix product states
papers.abstract: Tensor networks and specifically matrix product states (MPS) enable feasible classical quantum circuit simulation when entanglement remains compressible, but for this, gate updates must balance accuracy, representation size, and runtime. Conventional methods incorporate a complete gate into the MPS before compressing enlarged bonds. Here, we instead use lessons from the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) to analyze the projected action of each gate on the MPS by reducing it to a continuous generator path. We establish the spatial and state-space structure of this projected evolution and show that both the fixed-rank and two-site actions are confined to a contiguous window spanned by the gate while retaining boundary information from the surrounding MPS. Within this window characterization, we delineate when the instantaneous two-site action is exact and when variational directions can block it completely. Using standard nearest-point-projection geometry, we also show that fixed-rank TDVP and the local nearest fixed-rank projection of the exact gate endpoint agree to first order. We implement the gate-window restriction with rank-adaptive two-site TDVP and test both the projected update and a hybrid method that reserves it for long-range gates. Across the circuit benchmarks, these implementations incur runtime overhead and show no consistent accuracy--cost advantage over the tested baseline methods. The resulting framework provides a gate-specific structural analysis and a tested implementation together with explicit limits on its practical performance.

papers.title: Salvetti complexes for conditional oriented matroids
papers.abstract: We give a new proof of the fact that the complement of the complexification of a real hyperplane arrangement is homotopy equivalent to the Salvetti complex of the associated oriented matroid. Our proof involves no choices, is relatively easy to visualize, and generalizes to the setting of conditional oriented matroids.

papers.title: The Polyhedral Structure of Energy Storage Operations: Convex Hull and Valid Inequalities
papers.abstract: Energy storage models rely on complementarity constraints to prevent simultaneous charging and discharging, which turn them into disjunctive, nonconvex programs. Their linear relaxations, widely used in power system operation and planning, often violate these constraints. This paper studies the polyhedral structure of the multi-period operational set of a storage unit with conversion losses. We characterize the extreme points of its convex hull and show that, over any sub-horizon, the maximum energy that can be charged, or discharged, during a subset of periods is a submodular function of that subset, computable by a greedy rule. This structure yields an exponential family of linear valid inequalities, which we strengthen with the continuous power variables, and for which we establish necessary and sufficient conditions to define facets of the convex hull. The family contains inequalities that strictly dominate the storage capacity inequalities available in the literature. We further develop a separation algorithm that computes all the coefficients of a cut in linear time and can be made exact over contiguous sets of periods, together with a lifting procedure for the cuts that fail a facet condition. In 2000 instances of energy arbitrage with negative prices, the linear relaxation strengthened with the separated cuts returns an optimal schedule, free of simultaneous charging and discharging, in every instance, mostly after a single round of separation, whereas the strongest linear relaxation in the literature charges and discharges simultaneously in 43% to 77% of them.

papers.title: A Quasi-experimental Study of Conversational AI-supported Engagement in Large CS Courses
papers.abstract: Lucrative career prospects and creative opportunities often attract students to enroll in computer science courses, resulting in large class sizes. A common challenge in large classrooms is the lack of engagement between students and both the instructor and the learning material. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) present an opportunity to leverage Conversational Artificial Intelligence (CAI) to address this challenge. To examine the potential of CAI to support engagement with learning material, we designed an in class activity in a large Software Engineering course in which students interacted with a CAI tool. Using a quasi-experimental, within-subject study design in a real classroom at a large public United States University. We compared student engagement during an activity that involved the use of CAI for discussion with an activity that did not (peer discussion). For our analysis, we collected data on students interactions with the CAI tool and their self-reported responses on multiple engagement scales. Results show higher student engagement with the learning material in the activity involving CAI discussion as opposed to without (peer discussion). Higher self-reported learning was also observed in the activity with CAI as compared to without. Students also reported significantly more usefulness for learning in the CAI condition. Overall, our results indicate that CAI (ChatGPT) has the potential to support engagement with learning content during in-class activities in large class sizes.

papers.title: Atoms, Worldlines, and the Scalar Approximation
papers.abstract: The worldline path-integral method, developed thus far for scalar fields, offers promising computational efficiency in general geometries, However, it relies so far on the scalar approximation that decomposes electromagnetic waves into two independent polarizations. In this work, we investigate different theoretical frameworks of fluctuation-induced effects and analyze the limitations of the worldline path-integral method in modeling multiple-atom Casimir-Polder interactions. In particular, we ask the question: how accurate is the scalar approximation? Using the worldline approach, it appears that a simple sum of the contributions from the two polarizations agrees with the exact Casimir-Polder force for two-atom systems. However, it turns out that this agreement is fortuitous. To enable calculations beyond two atoms via worldlines, we develop general N-atom expressions for the Casimir-Polder force within the scalar approximation. For three-body systems, the scalar worldline method fails drastically, predicting significant discrepancies in both magnitude and sign due to strong polarization mixing. Furthermore, we show that the TE/TM decomposition in the worldline method differs from that of the Green-tensor formalism, and we discuss why this is. This study highlights the inadequacy of scalar worldline models that rely on the polarization-decomposition approximation in general geometries.

papers.title: Dressed Subsystems in Classical Gravity
papers.abstract: This paper considers the problem of consistently defining subsystems in gravitational theories. It is argued that a subsystem is a spacetime subregion in which the observables form a closed Poisson algebra. In a generally covariant theory, the location of the subregion must be determined in relation to other degrees of freedom. It is proposed that these degrees of freedom should live within the region, so that an observer can determine its edge by only measuring fields inside of it. This turns out to be equivalent to the property that observables in the subregion generate field-dependent gauge transformations on the causal complement. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this is \textit{exactly} what is necessary for the observables to form a Poisson algebra and thus to constitute a consistent subsystem. Observables in spacelike separated "dressed subsystems" are shown to commute. Several examples are given in the context of General Relativity. Along the way, new perspectives on the covariant phase space formalism are introduced that clarify well-known issues, such as the factorization of subregions in gauge theories and the unambiguous definition of Noether charges associated with one-sided boosts. Finally, prospects for extending these results to a perturbative quantum setting are discussed.

papers.title: Symbolic powers of the generic linkage of maximal minors
papers.abstract: Let $I$ be the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a matrix of indeterminates over a field and let $J$ denote the generic link, i.e., the most general link, of $I$. The generators of the ideal $J$ are not known in general. We provide an explicit description of the lead terms of the generators of $J$ using Gröbner degeneration. Indeed, we construct a degeneration which preserves the entire graded Betti table of $J$ on passing to the initial ideal. We leverage this construction to establish the equality of the symbolic and ordinary powers of $J$. Our analysis of the initial ideal readily yields the Gorenstein property of the associated graded ring of $J$, and, in positive characteristic, the $F$-rationality of the Rees algebra of $J$. Using the technique of $F$-split filtrations, we further establish the $F$-regularity of these blowup algebras.

papers.title: HDR-GS: Efficient High Dynamic Range Novel View Synthesis at 1000x Speed via Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: High dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) aims to create photorealistic images from novel viewpoints using HDR imaging techniques. The rendered HDR images capture a wider range of brightness levels containing more details of the scene than normal low dynamic range (LDR) images. Existing HDR NVS methods are mainly based on NeRF. They suffer from long training time and slow inference speed. In this paper, we propose a new framework, High Dynamic Range Gaussian Splatting (HDR-GS), which can efficiently render novel HDR views and reconstruct LDR images with a user input exposure time. Specifically, we design a Dual Dynamic Range (DDR) Gaussian point cloud model that uses spherical harmonics to fit HDR color and employs an MLP-based tone-mapper to render LDR color. The HDR and LDR colors are then fed into two Parallel Differentiable Rasterization (PDR) processes to reconstruct HDR and LDR views. To establish the data foundation for the research of 3D Gaussian splatting-based methods in HDR NVS, we recalibrate the camera parameters and compute the initial positions for Gaussian point clouds. Experiments demonstrate that our HDR-GS surpasses the state-of-the-art NeRF-based method by 3.84 and 1.91 dB on LDR and HDR NVS while enjoying 1000x inference speed and only requiring 6.3% training time. Code and recalibrated data will be publicly available at this https URL . Our project page at this https URL shows more video and interactive results. An online Gradio demo is also available on HuggingFace at this https URL

papers.title: Braid: Sybil-Resistant Decentralized Identity with Trustless Key Recovery and Non-Transferable Anonymous Credentials
papers.abstract: Decentralized identity frameworks grant users full sovereignty over their digital assets in the Web3 ecosystem. However, allowing arbitrary creation of identifiers makes the system susceptible to Sybil attacks and puts assets at risk when keys are lost or compromised. Moreover, the lack of identification prevents anonymous credential schemes from deterring malicious transfers. Existing solutions link identifiers to entities through trusted intermediaries, which are not always accessible and require costly offline interactions. We introduce Braid, a decentralized identity system with Sybil resistance, trustless key recovery, and non-transferable anonymous credentials. Braid creates blockchain-based bindings between identifiers and gradually combines identifiers belonging to the same holder into a unified associated identifier. As all identifiers within an association are presumed to belong to one individual, any fraudulent activity can be detected. The association grows larger as interactions increase, substantially reducing the likelihood of successful Sybil attacks. This mechanism allows holders to recover identifiers with lost keys or partial key compromise by proving knowledge of specific association structures. Additionally, Braid prevents unauthorized transfers through blockchain-based identifier-key bindings and proofs of ownership for credentials. Compared with representative prior approaches that provide only campaign-scoped Sybil protection or stateless anonymous-credential presentation, Braid carries association state across applications, enabling progressive Sybil resistance and trustless recovery while preserving zero-knowledge credential presentation. The evaluation shows that Braid bridges privacy-preserving credentials and accountable identity, achieving identifier association and credential presentation times of 2.41s and 3.31s on consumer-grade devices.

papers.title: Active Learning For Contextual Linear Optimization: A Margin-Based Approach
papers.abstract: We develop the first active learning method for contextual linear optimization. Specifically, we introduce a label acquisition algorithm that sequentially decides whether to request the ``labels'' of feature samples arriving in an unlabeled data stream, where the labels correspond to the objective coefficients in the linear optimization problem. The label acquisition rule is guided by the decision loss induced by the predicted coefficients, known as the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss. Motivated by the structure of the SPO loss, our algorithm uses the distance to degeneracy as a margin-based criterion for label acquisition. The algorithm processes incoming feature samples in batches, acquiring within each batch only the labels of samples whose distance to degeneracy falls below a rejection threshold. We derive non-asymptotic bounds for direct SPO-loss minimization over a general hypothesis class and for surrogate-loss minimization over a linear prediction class. These bounds demonstrate that, under certain natural conditions, our margin-based active learning algorithm requires fewer labels than supervised learning to achieve the same excess population risk for the chosen training loss. We provide concrete examples in which these conditions hold under continuous (sub-)Gaussian noise. Finally, we present numerical evidence demonstrating the practical value of our approach in applications such as personalized pricing and shortest-path problems.
